metadata.abstract: The study investigates the ordinary repertory of Aquileia and Cividale, highlighting the German-Central European influence on their liturgical melodies, which contrasts with the broader Italian tradition. Through comparative analysis, the research identifies distinct groups of melodies, including those unique to the region and those shared with wider European traditions, while acknowledging the limitations of catalog data and the need for further exploration of chronological and contextual factors. The findings suggest a complex intercultural exchange in the Aquileian sources, emphasizing the importance of considering both geographical and temporal influences in liturgical studies.

For a survey of the ordinary repertory of Aquileia I used a coherent source group which can be seen in your handout,

After cataloguing all ordinary melodies in DEM, I analyzed what kind of melodies the repertories are compiled from and how they can be grouped, which melodies are Einzelmelodien, if there are any examples at all, and which appear more frequently in the sources. The latter requires further differentiation, for it is by no means indifferent what broad dissemination the information referred to, behind the individual melodies belonging to this group. The appearance of the general European repertory calls for an explanation less than that of regional or local melodies do. Finally, it is necessary to check whether observations concerning the dissemination of melodies indicate some trends, or whether it is possible to grasp the character of the source group under discussion, on the basis of DEM, at least in this repertory. Formulated in another way, is any kind of orientation palpable in the analyzed source group? Now let's take a look at concrete observations in the order of the dissemination of melodies. The comparative tables in example 2 show the content of the sources according to genre. First, Kyria melodies. And after that, Gloria, and so on. On the basis of this information, I have prepared a table with a grouping of melodies. Example 3.

In the first group, in example 3, I placed melodies that are documented in the catalogs from one source alone. The Sanctus melody, 189. This is an exception, since it occurs in three sources, but all from Cividale. Although, as concrete examples, we can regard this Einzelmelodien as characteristic of the area, or source group, under discussion, their number doesn't differ from the average of such melodies in other areas. For example, concerning Italy, Schildbach registers 26 such melodies, from the 11th to the 12th of the 19th century. In the comparative tables, I have marked the Einzelmelodien together with the melodies known only from Italian sources as underlined, as you can see in example 2.

In the second group of example 3, back to the example 3, I have collected melodies that were used all over Europe through the centuries, and which, according to the Encel Melodien, were used in the 19th and 20th centuries. These melodies, according to my information, became integral elements of the Aquileian tradition as well. Those well-known melodies that occur only exceptionally in Aquileia are placed in the next row of this table.

The original melodies are undoubtedly more interesting than those of the above-mentioned groups. The next two categories were not arbitrarily created but took shape almost automatically on the basis of collected information on the distribution of the melodies. In the sources of Aquileia we find a remarkably great number of melodies that were disseminated mainly in German and Central European manuscripts. In the comparative tables these are indicated in bold lettering. This observation seems to be of even greater importance by the fact that besides the German and Ostlandish sources using the term of the catalogues they occur mostly or exclusively in Aquileia and codices.
So, not in other Italian manuscripts. On the basis of their dissemination in Italian sources the items of this group can be differentiated further as can be seen in example 4.

Among these German-oriented melodies, we find only one that proves to be widely disseminated in Italian regions. Beyond numerous north Italian sources, this Kyrian number 151 occurs in Beneventan manuscripts as well. It is striking that beside the overall similarity in their orientation, the sources from Aquileia and Cividale do not agree with each other in every respect. For example, while the Gloria number 48 occurs only in sources from Cividale, the Kyrian melodies number 144 or number 74 can be exclusively documented from Aquileia.

Camillo Oswald emphasizes in the above-mentioned monograph that the origin of Aquileia does not coincide with that of Cividale, and that, although the diocesan repertoire is uniformly overlaid, it does not coincide in all points. The observations in the ordinary repertory, which will be summarized later on, indicate that, in the case of the diocesan repertoire, they agree with these formulations.

Though in the Aquileia and Cividale the general and central European melodies represent the majority in the presence of a few other melodies, a different influence reveals itself. The fifth row of the third example contains melodies, the dissemination of which can be regarded as the inverse of that of the previous group. While they are generally unknown or at least exceptional in German sources, apart from more or less Italian manuscripts, they are well represented among French and sometimes English and Sicilian sources. These are indicated in italic lettering in the comparative table.
It is remarkable that inside my Aquileian source group these appear exceptionally in a source that was categorized as Benedictine in the catalogues, this is that Berlin source.

Now, let us examine in detail the relationship between the Aquileian sources, in the narrow sense, and the sources from Cividale. On the basis of the comparative tables, we can declare that at least the Kyrie and Gloria melodies offer sufficient reference points, which show a close relationship between the sources of the two chapters. See example 5.

In the light of these observations, we can interpret the differences and inconsistencies of the Sanctus or Agnus Dei repertories as capriciousness in the recording of the melodies. For example, in the case of the strikingly rich repertory of the source, Udine, 93, see example 2, we cannot simply decide whether we are faced with an additional extra material in the source, or a missing portion of the repertory in the case of the other sources. In any case, the majority of these extra melodies give the impression that we are faced with an additional extra material in the source, and give evidence of the above-mentioned German orientation as well.

Perhaps the most notable observation is that the German Ostländisch or Ostfrankisch, I would say, orientation reveals itself on a more general level than that of the inner differentiation of the diocese. Such melodies prevail not only in the common stock of melodies, but among the local ones too. So, the melodies were in use either only in Aquileia or only in Cividale. Formulated in another way, the source groups of Aquileia, in the narrow sense, and Cividale reveal a German-Central European orientation also independently of each other. It is frequently emphasized in the literature that besides indications of a connection between Aquileia and the neighboring Italias, the influence of the northern areas can be strongly felt. This may be attributed to several factors, the listing of which would exceed the limits of this paper. Suffice it to mention the intercultural position of this area, the fact that between the 11th and 13th centuries all patriarchs were of German origin, or the influence of the Italian monasteries founded from here-so, etc. The many experiences referring to this, served as a basis for the view that research should concentrate on an identification of evidence of this German influence, rather than the definition of an independent and, to a certain extent, imaginary Aquileian liturgy. In any case, an examination of the ordinary repertory of Aquileia coincides with these observations.

A comparative analysis of the Kyriale repertories of the sources raises another critical question. The claim arises naturally that we should check the former observations by comparing the Aquileian sources with carefully selected Italian sources from the neighboring or possibly more remote regions. For this reason, I have made further analysis in the following source group, see example 6. The first of the two subgroups, which I separated in the following comparative tables too, contains North Italian while the other has rather Central Italian sources. Of course, in the arbitrariness or one might say haphazardness in the selection of sources, a certain danger is concealed. Nevertheless, on the basis of a relatively large number of instances, the characteristic points reveal themselves and confirm the relative independence of the Aquileian source group. Some of these characteristic points connect to a wide circle of Italian sources to each other, while others serve as a basis for further differentiation. And what is more important, the similarities and differences can be interpreted along the same trends as those which are used in the study of the Aquileian sources. In the Aquileian repertory, that is, the somewhat abstract and hypothetical methodological categories concerning the orientation of sources prove to be useful here as well. The number of the Einzelmelodien doesn't differ from general experience though there are significant differences between the individual sources in this respect. For example, one of the Piacenza sources, this one is the number 65, excels the others with its nine such melodies. Where the widespread European repertory is concerned, we find here largely the same items from it as in Aquileia. However, the situation is completely different in the cases of the Italian and regionally disseminated ordinary melodies. I discuss them respectively. See now example 8. It is strikingly clear, that the melodies sometimes well represented, though not equally, in north and central Italian sources were not in use in Aquileia at all. The one exception is the Kyrie melody number 31, which besides the source from San Marco can also be documented from Monza, Benevent, Monte Cassino and Nursia as well. The number of the so-called German, German-oriented melodies is remarkably less than was in Aquileia. This is more significant in the light of the dissemination since here such melodies occur sporadically here and there. An exception is the Gloria 19, which on the other hand is missing from Aquileian sources, though this is also a German-oriented melody well known in Central Europe and Italy.

The high number of melodies hypothetically called West Frankish is completely in harmony with this observation. Although some of them can be documented from one or a few sources, which may be a consequence of the random selection of the sources, others show themselves significantly characteristic of the non-Aquileian Italian codices. I have marked them with an asterisk in the third row of example A.
